question: In the negotiations on the free trade agreement between the EU and the Philippines, special attention should be paid to a sector as sensitive as the European tuna processing industry, which is a strategic sector and very important to a number of coastal communities. It is labour-intensive, creates a large number of jobs and processes some 340 000 tonnes a year.

The Philippines is a very competitive player in the global tuna sector and has the potential to get significantly stronger. It is currently the chief Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) exporter of canned tuna to the EU.

Granting trade preferences to the Philippines – on top of those already granted or provided for in other agreements – would increase pressure on the European processing industry, in a market where imports already account for around 50% of consumption. Against this backdrop, and taking into account that the Commission is aware of the importance of this sector: 1.
Is the Commission considering maintaining tuna’s status as a sensitive product in the negotiations with the Philippines?
Has it carried out or does it intend to carry out an assessment on the impact of liberalising imports of preserved Filipino tuna into the European processing industry?
Would an assessment take account of the cumulative effects of other agreements – such as the one recently concluded with Mexico – and preferential arrangements?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.7.2026) The negotiations for a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) with the Philippines are ongoing. So far, six rounds of negotiations have taken place. The Commission aims for an ambitious, comprehensive and modern agreement that can create opportunities for EU businesses while carefully handling sensitivities and potential impacts on particular sectors.

Throughout the negotiations, the Commission shares with the co-legislators all the EU’s text proposals and market access offers and maintains regular contacts with stakeholders. The Philippines is a beneficiary of the Generalised Scheme of Preferences + arrangement, under which it has enjoyed duty-free, quota-free access for tuna products for over a decade, with stable export volumes over that period.
Therefore, the FTA would not open a new flow into the EU market but, at most, consolidate an existing one. Tuna remains sensitive in the negotiations, and the Commission is handling it accordingly.

The Commission will take into account the interests of the EU fleet and processing industry, the current and potential impact of imports, and the cumulative effect on the EU market of preferential access granted under other agreements and arrangements, in order to achieve a balanced outcome.
